Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p ≥ .25", "p > .05"), Sentence = c("All plots for homoscedasticity and normality of residues were found to be inconspicuous; Shapiro-Wilk tests on the residuals were non-significant for all six models (all W ≥ .98, all p ≥ .25).", "Neither L2 English oral reading rate nor accuracy was significantly predicted by any of the variables included in the linear mixed model (all p > .05)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 1 data file could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: Scientific articles usually go through a peer-review process.

Please note that the present article has not (yet) undergone this standard procedure for scientific publications.

Reading and spelling are foundational skills for academic success in both firstlanguage (L1) (e.g., National Reading Panel, 2000) and second-language (L2foot_0 ) contexts (August & Shanahan, 2006), enabling children to access and participate fully in the wider curriculum.
text.formatted: Reading and spelling are foundational skills for academic success in both firstlanguage (L1) <ref type="bibr">(e.g., National Reading Panel, 2000)</ref> and second-language (L2<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> ) contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(August & Shanahan, 2006)</ref>, enabling children to access and participate fully in the wider curriculum.

text.text: Research in English-majority contexts has identified both cognitive and linguistic factors that underlie these skills in children L2 learning.

Phonological short-term memory (PSTM) and phonological awareness (PA), as well as grammar and vocabulary knowledge, are associated with L2 English reading (Chen et al., 2015; Grabe & Yamashita, 2022) and spelling (e.g., Keilty & Harrison, 2015; Zaretsky, 2020).
text.formatted: Phonological short-term memory (PSTM) and phonological awareness (PA), as well as grammar and vocabulary knowledge, are associated with L2 English reading <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Chen et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Grabe & Yamashita, 2022)</ref> and spelling (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Keilty & Harrison, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Zaretsky, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Far less is known about whether these findings hold in English as a foreign language (EFL) contexts, where children learn English mainly in the classroom and have limited language exposure.

In such contexts, studies have reported inconsistent results regarding the influence of precursory skillssuch as phonological awarenesson reading (e.g., Huo & Wang, 2017) and spelling skills in EFL learners (Mlakar et al., 2025a (Mlakar et al., , 2025b;; Russak, 2020).
text.formatted: In such contexts, studies have reported inconsistent results regarding the influence of precursory skillssuch as phonological awarenesson reading (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Huo & Wang, 2017)</ref> and spelling skills in EFL learners <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Mlakar et al., 2025a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Mlakar et al., , 2025b;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Russak, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, few studies examine cognitive and linguistic predictors together, across reading and spelling, and for both real words and pseudowords, which would show whether different skills support lexical and non-lexical processing.
The German context also raises a question of transfer.

German has a relatively shallow orthography with highly consistent grapheme-phoneme correspondences, whereas English is deep, characterized by ambiguous sound-spelling mappings and unique phonemes that do not exist in the German phonological inventory (Landerl, 2005; Schmalz et al., 2015).

text.text: According to the Linguistic Coding Differences Hypothesis (Sparks & Ganschow, 1991) and accounts of cross-language transfer (Geva & Siegel, 2000; Geva & Yaghoub Zadeh, 2006), L1-indexed phonological and cognitive skills should nevertheless relate to L2 literacy.

text.text: However, these differences between the two orthographies may limit how directly such skills transfer to English.

The present study therefore examines how nonverbal intelligence (NVI), PSTM, PA, working memory (WM), and L2 English grammar and vocabulary knowledge relate to L2 English reading (comprehension, oral reading rate and accuracy, pseudoword reading) and spelling (real words and pseudowords) among EFL elementary school learners in Germany.
The aim is to clarify the cognitive and linguistic foundations of L2 literacy in a low-exposure context and to inform both theoretical models of literacy acquisition and EFL instruction.
The present study draws on established theoretical models of reading and spelling to examine the predictors of literacy attainment in EFL learners.

Specifically, the framework integrates perspectives on (a) reading comprehension, guided by the Simple View of Reading Turning first to reading comprehension (a), it is widely recognized as one of the most crucial foundations of academic achievement.
Reading comprehension involves the integration of diverse cognitive and linguistic skills, making its development a complex process that has prompted the formulation of various theoretical models.
A foundational perspective is offered by the SVR (Gough & Tunmer, 1986; Hoover & Gough, 1990), which conceptualizes reading comprehension as the joint product of decoding and language comprehension.
text.formatted: A foundational perspective is offered by the SVR <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Gough & Tunmer, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Hoover & Gough, 1990)</ref>, which conceptualizes reading comprehension as the joint product of decoding and language comprehension.

text.text: SVR is a widely used and influential model in reading research, with substantial empirical support across languages, orthographies, and learner populationsincluding L2 and EFL contexts (Lee et al., 2022).
text.formatted: SVR is a widely used and influential model in reading research, with substantial empirical support across languages, orthographies, and learner populationsincluding L2 and EFL contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Lee et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Reading (DIER; Kim, 2017) has expanded the SVR and highlights the contributions of foundational language skills (e.g., vocabulary and grammatical knowledge), upper-level language skills (e.g., word reading and listening comprehension), and cognitive abilities (e.g., WM) to reading comprehension outcomes.
text.formatted: The Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Reading (DIER; <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Kim, 2017)</ref> has expanded the SVR and highlights the contributions of foundational language skills (e.g., vocabulary and grammatical knowledge), upper-level language skills (e.g., word reading and listening comprehension), and cognitive abilities (e.g., WM) to reading comprehension outcomes.

text.text: Core language resources support the construction of an initial textbase representation, enabling learners to understand word meanings and sentence structures.
Building on this linguistic foundation, cognitive skills such as WM play a pivotal role in integrating and manipulating linguistic information during reading (e.g., Chen et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Building on this linguistic foundation, cognitive skills such as WM play a pivotal role in integrating and manipulating linguistic information during reading (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Chen et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The DIER model is especially useful in contexts such as EFL, where limited L2 exposure and weaker decoding skills can make vocabulary and grammar particularly salient predictors of reading comprehension.
Empirical studies consistently indicate that, during the initial years of schooling, decoding skills explain most of the variance in reading comprehension outcomes (Catts, 2018).
text.formatted: Empirical studies consistently indicate that, during the initial years of schooling, decoding skills explain most of the variance in reading comprehension outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Catts, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: As learners advance, however, foundational language skillsparticularly L2 receptive vocabulary (r = .79) and L2 grammar knowledge (r = .85)become increasingly prominent predictors of L2 reading comprehension outcomes (Jeon & Yamashita, 2014).
text.formatted: As learners advance, however, foundational language skillsparticularly L2 receptive vocabulary (r = .79) and L2 grammar knowledge (r = .85)become increasingly prominent predictors of L2 reading comprehension outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Jeon & Yamashita, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: These findings support a theoretical framework in which cognitive resources (e.g., WM) and linguistic resources (e.g., vocabulary and grammar) are conceptualized as complementary foundations of reading comprehension, particularly in the context of L2 learning and among developing readers (Juffs & Harrington, 2011; Vettori et al., 2024).
text.formatted: These findings support a theoretical framework in which cognitive resources (e.g., WM) and linguistic resources (e.g., vocabulary and grammar) are conceptualized as complementary foundations of reading comprehension, particularly in the context of L2 learning and among developing readers <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Juffs & Harrington, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Vettori et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Turning to (b) reading fluency: While models of reading comprehension emphasize the interaction of linguistic and cognitive processes in constructing meaning, complementary perspectives focus on the fluency with which these processes are executed.

Within second language acquisition frameworks, automaticity theory (DeKeyser, 2001; Segalowitz, 2003) emphasizes the importance of efficient, accurate, and rapid word recognition as a foundation for fluent reading.
text.formatted: Within second language acquisition frameworks, automaticity theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(DeKeyser, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Segalowitz, 2003)</ref> emphasizes the importance of efficient, accurate, and rapid word recognition as a foundation for fluent reading.

text.text: Within reading research, fluency is typically defined as the ability to translate written text into oral language with both speed and accuracy.

It is widely regarded as a key indicator of the extent to which reading sub-processessuch as phonological decoding, word recognition, and syntactic parsinghave become automatized and well-coordinated in the L2 (Grabe, 2010).
text.formatted: It is widely regarded as a key indicator of the extent to which reading sub-processessuch as phonological decoding, word recognition, and syntactic parsinghave become automatized and well-coordinated in the L2 <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Grabe, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Both oral and silent reading fluency are considered critical, as fluent reading reflects the successful integration of lower-level processes and provides the cognitive efficiency needed to support higher-level comprehension (Grabe & Yamashita, 2022).
text.formatted: Both oral and silent reading fluency are considered critical, as fluent reading reflects the successful integration of lower-level processes and provides the cognitive efficiency needed to support higher-level comprehension <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Grabe & Yamashita, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: For EFL learners, these processes have to be (re-)automatized in English, regardless of L1 reading skill, because orthographic and phonological processing are language-specific (Koda, 2005).
text.formatted: For EFL learners, these processes have to be (re-)automatized in English, regardless of L1 reading skill, because orthographic and phonological processing are language-specific <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Koda, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: In this framework, reading fluency functions not only as an outcome of the acquisitional progress in decoding and word recognition, but also as a bridge to successful comprehension.

This dual role makes reading fluency a central component of L2 literacy development, which is particularly relevant in EFL contexts where learners must allocate substantial cognitive resources to both speed and accuracy of processing.
Although much of the foundational fluency research has stemmed from English L1 contexts, a growing body of work in L2 and EFL settings affirms the central role that fluency plays for L2 learners.

For example, research suggests that oral reading fluencymeasured in terms of rate and accuracy, as in the study at handis associated with both vocabulary development and reading comprehension among L2 readers (Grabe, 2010; Jeon, 2012; Taguchi & Gorsuch, 2012).
text.formatted: For example, research suggests that oral reading fluencymeasured in terms of rate and accuracy, as in the study at handis associated with both vocabulary development and reading comprehension among L2 readers <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Grabe, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Jeon, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Taguchi & Gorsuch, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Psycholinguistic models of L2 development emphasize that building fluency allows learners to process larger linguistic units more rapidly and with greater accuracy, thus supporting overall reading proficiency in a foreign language (Segalowitz, 2003).
text.formatted: Psycholinguistic models of L2 development emphasize that building fluency allows learners to process larger linguistic units more rapidly and with greater accuracy, thus supporting overall reading proficiency in a foreign language <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Segalowitz, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, with respect to (c) spelling and pseudoword reading, the present study's focus is informed by the Dual-Route Cascaded model (e.g., Barry, 1994; Coltheart et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Finally, with respect to (c) spelling and pseudoword reading, the present study's focus is informed by the Dual-Route Cascaded model (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Barry, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Coltheart et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: This model distinguishes between two primary pathways in reading and spelling: the lexical (direct) route and the sublexical (indirect) route.

The lexical route provides direct access to stored word representations in the mental lexicon, supporting rapid recognition and accurate spelling of familiar words, including those with irregular or unpredictable graphemephoneme correspondences.

By contrast, the sublexical route relies on the serial application of grapheme-phoneme conversion rules, enabling learners to decode or spell unfamiliar words and pseudowords by systematically mapping letters onto sounds.
This route is essential for processing novel words or orthographic patterns not yet stored in the mental lexicon, making it particularly relevant for tasks involving pseudoword reading and spelling.
Building on these theoretical frameworks, the following section reviews empirical evidence regarding cognitive and linguistic predictors of EFL reading.
Cognitive abilities have received increasing attention as predictors of individual differences in L2 reading outcomes.
Among the cognitive predictors, PA has received particular attention.
PA refers to the ability to perceive, identify, and manipulate the sound structure of spoken language at different grain sizes, including syllables, onsets and rimes, and phonemes.

While PA is widely recognized as a foundational skill for word reading in L1 English (e.g., Melby-Lervåg et al., 2012), its impact on EFL and English as a Second Language (ESL) word reading appears to be more moderate (Murphy Odo, 2021), and evidence for a direct contribution to EFL reading comprehension remains limited (Huo & Wang, 2017).
text.formatted: While PA is widely recognized as a foundational skill for word reading in L1 English (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Melby-Lervåg et al., 2012)</ref>, its impact on EFL and English as a Second Language (ESL) word reading appears to be more moderate (Murphy Odo, 2021), and evidence for a direct contribution to EFL reading comprehension remains limited <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Huo & Wang, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, both studies provide strong evidence that PA is a key predictor of L2 pseudoword (or nonword) reading accuracy, as advanced PA skills facilitate the application of grapheme-phoneme correspondence rules to unfamiliar letter strings.
However, transfer from L1 German PA to L2 English reading is not necessarily straightforward.

Core aspects of PA, such as the ability to identify, segment, and manipulate phonological units, are considered language-general and may transfer across alphabetic languages (Melby-Lervåg & Lervåg, 2011).
text.formatted: Core aspects of PA, such as the ability to identify, segment, and manipulate phonological units, are considered language-general and may transfer across alphabetic languages <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Melby-Lervåg & Lervåg, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, German and English differ substantially in orthographic depth and phonological structure.

German has relatively consistent grapheme-phoneme correspondences for reading, whereas English is less transparent and requires learners to deal with inconsistent mappings, larger grain-size units, and language-specific orthographic patterns such as vowel and consonant digraphs, or silent-letter patterns (Landerl, 2005; Seymour et al., 2003).
text.formatted: German has relatively consistent grapheme-phoneme correspondences for reading, whereas English is less transparent and requires learners to deal with inconsistent mappings, larger grain-size units, and language-specific orthographic patterns such as vowel and consonant digraphs, or silent-letter patterns <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Landerl, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Seymour et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, English includes phonemes and contrasts that are absent or less salient in German, such as /θ/or /ð/.
These differences may constrain how directly L1 phonological skills can be applied to English word and pseudoword reading.
Thus, although PA is a robust predictor of pseudoword reading, its contribution may vary depending on the structural and phonological overlap between the L1 and L2.

This assumption is consistent with the Linguistic Coding Differences Hypothesis (Sparks & Ganschow, 1991), which proposes that individual differences in foreign-language learning partly reflect learners' established L1 linguistic coding abilities.
text.formatted: This assumption is consistent with the Linguistic Coding Differences Hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Sparks & Ganschow, 1991)</ref>, which proposes that individual differences in foreign-language learning partly reflect learners' established L1 linguistic coding abilities.

text.text: From this perspective, phonological abilities assessed in the L1 may provide resources for L2 reading.
PSTM is another cognitive factor implicated in L2 literacy.

It supports the temporary maintenance of phonological information, which is relevant when learners decode unfamiliar words and when they hold spoken or written language in mind during comprehension (Farnia & Geva, 2013; Walter, 2008).
text.formatted: It supports the temporary maintenance of phonological information, which is relevant when learners decode unfamiliar words and when they hold spoken or written language in mind during comprehension <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Farnia & Geva, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Walter, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: PSTM has been linked to pseudoword reading accuracy (Geva & Siegel, 2000; Geva & Yaghoub Zadeh, 2006).
text.formatted: PSTM has been linked to pseudoword reading accuracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Geva & Siegel, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Geva & Yaghoub Zadeh, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: The strength of this association may depend on how PSTM is measured.

Nonword repetition draws on the sound structure of a specific language and is therefore more language-sensitive, whereas digit span relies on highly familiar items and is likely to index a more language-general capacity (Gathercole & Baddeley, 1990).
text.formatted: Nonword repetition draws on the sound structure of a specific language and is therefore more language-sensitive, whereas digit span relies on highly familiar items and is likely to index a more language-general capacity <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Gathercole & Baddeley, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, PSTM was assessed with a digit span task in L1 German.
WM and NVI are two further cognitive resources linked to L2 reading comprehension, although the evidence for WM is mixed.

According to Kim's (2017) DIER model, WM allows readers to hold and manipulate linguistic information during sentence and discourse processing, which supports inference generation and the integration of information across clauses.
text.formatted: According to <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Kim's (2017)</ref> DIER model, WM allows readers to hold and manipulate linguistic information during sentence and discourse processing, which supports inference generation and the integration of information across clauses.

text.text: A meta-analysis found moderate associations between WM and several reading components (Peng et al., 2018), and positive associations with L2 reading comprehension have been reported in children and adults (Farnia & Geva, 2013; Jeon & Yamashita, 2014; Juffs & Harrington, 2011; Vettori et al., 2024).
text.formatted: A meta-analysis found moderate associations between WM and several reading components <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Peng et al., 2018)</ref>, and positive associations with L2 reading comprehension have been reported in children and adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Farnia & Geva, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Jeon & Yamashita, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Juffs & Harrington, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Vettori et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Other findings are less consistent, however.

Meta-analyses show that the WM-L2 reading relationship varies with methodological factors such as the language of the WM task, measurement reliability, and task type (In'nami et al., 2022; Shin, 2020).
text.formatted: Meta-analyses show that the WM-L2 reading relationship varies with methodological factors such as the language of the WM task, measurement reliability, and task type <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(In'nami et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Shin, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: NVI, often understood as fluid reasoning ability (e.g., Schneider & McGrew, 2018), may support comprehension through abstract thinking, pattern recognition, and the construction of situation models from text, particularly when vocabulary and background knowledge are limited, as is common in EFL learners (e.g., Motallebzadeh & Tabatabaee Yazdi, 2016).

text.text: Importantly, the predictive value of both constructs may also reflect their shared cognitive basis.

A large body of research suggests that the limited capacity of WM (i.e., working memory capacity) is strongly associated with measures of reasoning ability (Kyllonen & Christal, 1990; Oberauer et al., 2005), which is often measured using non-verbal scales like figural matrices (e.g., Raven, 1990).
text.formatted: A large body of research suggests that the limited capacity of WM (i.e., working memory capacity) is strongly associated with measures of reasoning ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Kyllonen & Christal, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Oberauer et al., 2005)</ref>, which is often measured using non-verbal scales like figural matrices (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Raven, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the predictive effects of both WM and NVI on L2 reading comprehension reported in the literature may reflect their shared underlying mechanism, rather than two distinct sources of cognitive support.

Although not assessed in the present study, rapid automatized naming (RAN) is a well-established predictor of reading fluency, as it indexes the speed of retrieving phonological codes for familiar visual symbols, a process that underlies efficient word recognition (e.g., Geva & Yaghoub Zadeh, 2006).

text.text: Beyond cognitive factors, linguistic resources play a crucial role in ESL and EFL reading comprehension and fluency.

L2 vocabulary knowledge is a well-established predictor of reading comprehension, as lexical knowledge provides the foundation for accessing and constructing meaning from text (Nation, 2009; Vettori et al., 2024; Yamashita, 2022; Zhang & Zhang, 2020).
text.formatted: L2 vocabulary knowledge is a well-established predictor of reading comprehension, as lexical knowledge provides the foundation for accessing and constructing meaning from text <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Nation, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Vettori et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Yamashita, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Zhang & Zhang, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: A robust vocabulary also facilitates the rapid and accurate recognition of words, thereby supporting greater reading fluency (Grabe, 2010; Jeon, 2012; Taguchi & Gorsuch, 2012).
text.formatted: A robust vocabulary also facilitates the rapid and accurate recognition of words, thereby supporting greater reading fluency <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Grabe, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Jeon, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Taguchi & Gorsuch, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: In addition to vocabulary, L2 grammatical knowledge has been shown to make an independent contribution to reading comprehension (Jeon & Yamashita, 2014; Vettori et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In addition to vocabulary, L2 grammatical knowledge has been shown to make an independent contribution to reading comprehension <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Jeon & Yamashita, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Vettori et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Orthographic knowledge, that is, familiarity with the letter patterns and spelling conventions of a writing system, is a further key resource, particularly for reading fluency and spelling.

According to the self-teaching hypothesis (Share, 1995), each successful decoding of an unfamiliar word helps readers build word-specific orthographic representations, which support fast and accurate word recognition (Ehri, 2014) and, in turn, spelling.
text.formatted: According to the self-teaching hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Share, 1995)</ref>, each successful decoding of an unfamiliar word helps readers build word-specific orthographic representations, which support fast and accurate word recognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Ehri, 2014)</ref> and, in turn, spelling.

text.text: Research on the predictors of L2 spelling comes mainly from North American ESL contexts, and evidence on young learners in non-immersive EFL settings is scarce.
Among cognitive skills, PA is the one most consistently linked to L2 spelling.

Stronger PA has been associated with more accurate spelling in ESL learners, particularly in the early stages of learning, when children must master unfamiliar phoneme-grapheme correspondences (Harrison et al., 2016; Jongejan et al., 2007; Keilty & Harrison, 2015; Yeung et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Stronger PA has been associated with more accurate spelling in ESL learners, particularly in the early stages of learning, when children must master unfamiliar phoneme-grapheme correspondences <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Harrison et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Jongejan et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Keilty & Harrison, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Yeung et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: PSTM may support the retention of novel phonological sequences and thus the spelling of unfamiliar words (Baddeley et al., 1998), and nonword repetition has been linked to spelling accuracy in young ESL learners (Zaretsky, 2020).

text.text: The contributions of WM and NVI are less clear.

Models of writing assign WM a role in coordinating orthographic, phonological, and morphological information (Hayes, 1996; Kellogg et al., 2013), but its specific contribution to L2 spelling accuracy has received little attention (Kormos, 2023).

text.text: For NVI, direct L2 evidence is lacking, but L1 studies have linked it to early spelling in English-speaking (Caravolas et al., 2001) and German-speaking children (Schneider & Niklas, 2017; Zarić et al., 2021).

text.text: Among linguistic predictors, vocabulary is a key correlate of general EFL writing proficiency (Miralpeix & Muñoz, 2018).

text.text: It may also support spelling, because mapping sounds onto letters is aided by knowledge of a word's meaning and by orthographic learning through repeated, meaningful exposure.

Evidence for grammar is inconsistent, partly because "grammar" is defined and measured differently across studies: syntactic knowledge predicted spelling in Canadian ESL kindergarteners (Keilty & Harrison, 2015), but other studies found no association (Harrison et al., 2016; Jongejan et al., 2007).

text.text: Whether and how linguistic knowledge contributes to EFL spelling therefore remains open.

Little is known about how cognitive and linguistic skills predict specific literacy outcomes in young EFL learners in Germany, who begin formal English instruction in Grade 3 (age 8-9), often before their L1 literacy is fully established.

The present study therefore examines to what extent cognitive skills (NVI, PSTM, PA, WM) and linguistic skills (L2 receptive grammar and vocabulary), assessed at the beginning of Grade 3, predict six L2 English literacy outcomes at the end of Grade 4: reading comprehension, pseudoword reading, oral reading rate and accuracy, and real-word and pseudoword spelling.
More specifically, we addressed four main research questions.

text.text: To what extent do cognitive abilities (NVI, PSTM, PA, WM) and linguistic skills (L2 grammar and vocabulary) at the beginning of Grade 3 predict L2 English reading comprehension at the end of Grade 4?

Based on the Simple View of Reading and its extensions (Gough & Tunmer, 1986; Kim, 2017), we expect that L2 vocabulary will be a strong predictor of reading comprehension (Nation, 2009; Vettori et al., 2024; Yamashita, 2022; Zhang & Zhang, 2020), with grammar knowledge possibly making an additional contribution (Jeon & Yamashita, 2014; Vettori et al., 2024).

text.text: Evidence for WM is mixed: it is theoretically relevant to integrating information in text (Farnia & Geva, 2013; Kim, 2017), but meta-analyses show that the WM-L2 reading relationship varies considerably (In'nami et al., 2022; Shin, 2020).

text.text: We therefore treat the role of WM as exploratory.
Which cognitive and linguistic skills predict L2 pseudoword reading?

text.text: Germanylearners received English lessons twice weekly (45 minutes per session).
The teaching approach in all classes followed a communicative language teaching framework and targeted all four primary language skills: listening, speaking, reading, and writing.
Parent questionnaires indicated that, before entering Grade 3, participants had very limited exposure to English.
Most of learners' contact with English came through L2 teacher input, the course textbooks, and supplementary materials such as children's books or audio resources.

Instruction followed Lower Saxony's elementary school English curriculum (Years 3-4) and the CEFR (Council of Europe, 2020), targeting A1 proficiency in listening, speaking, and reading, with writing approaching A1 by Year 4.
Our study employed a combination of reading, spelling, cognitive, and linguistic assessments for data collection.

Participants were monitored over a two-year period, beginning with the administration of cognitive and linguistic assessments (PA, PSTM, WM, NVI, vocabulary, grammar) at the start of Grade 3 and concluding with the reading and spelling assessments at the end of Grade 4.

Testing conditions were carefully controlled: PA, PSTM, WM, oral reading fluency, and pseudoword reading were assessed individually in quiet surroundings, while spelling, reading comprehension, vocabulary/grammar, and NVI measures were administered in group settings.
All instructions were provided in German to ensure consistency.
The data collection team comprised researchers and graduate students who had received formal training in the administration and scoring of the measures.

This study aimed to deepen our understanding of the foundational knowledge bases underlying early literacy skills in young EFL learners in Germany.
We examined the predictors of L2 English reading comprehension, pseudoword reading, oral reading fluency, and both real-word and pseudoword spelling.
Addressing research question 1 (predictors of L2 reading comprehension), NVI and PA emerged as robust cognitive predictors that held even after we accounted for the number of predictors tested.
L2 English vocabulary knowledge was a further predictor in the primary models, though one that did not reach significance after correction and therefore warrants investigation.

These findings suggest that both domain-general (NVI) and domain-specific (PA) skills make distinct contributions to early EFL reading comprehension, reflecting the demands of reading in a low-exposure context, where learners must coordinate developing that we assessed WM in German.

text.text: Turning to research question 2 (predictors of L2 pseudoword reading), PSTM was the only significant predictor of English pseudoword reading in the mixed-effects model.

The finding is consistent with the view that PSTM supports sublexical decoding by holding phonological representations in place (Gathercole & Baddeley, 1990) while graphemes are sequentially converted and blended into a whole-word pronunciation (Melby-Lervåg et al., 2012), and with dual-route models in which unfamiliar items are read via the sublexical (phonological) route (Coltheart et al., 2001).

With this caveat, our results suggest that L2 real-word spelling might depend on language-specific knowledge.

This aligns with models of spelling, which emphasize the integration of semantic, morphosyntactic, phonological, and orthographic knowledge (Apel et al., 2004; Treiman, 2017) and with Ehri's (2014) account of orthographic mapping, in which spellings are stored in memory as links between pronunciations, meanings, and letter sequences.

text.text: We propose that L2 vocabulary knowledge contributes to this process in two ways.
First, familiar words provide phonological and semantic representations that can support the retention of their spellings, whereas unknown words offer little to anchor them (Ehri, 2014; Share, 1995).

text.text: Second, lexical familiarity may facilitate the identification and segmentation of spoken word forms during dictation, particularly when these contain phonemes absent from German (e.g., /θ/, /ð/).
The relationship between L2 vocabulary and spelling has been documented in ESL contexts in North America (Jongejan et al., 2007; Zaretsky, 2020), but evidence from EFL contexts remains limited.

We suggest instead that the ELIAS grammar score may index general L2 proficiency, which may help learners apply English sound-spelling conventions, such as the representations of /æ/, /ɒ/, /θ/, /ð/, the digraph <sh>, and the silent-<e> pattern.

text.text: Moreover, the grammar score combined morphological and syntactic items, so we cannot determine which aspects of grammatical knowledge drove the effect.
Contrary to our hypothesis, PA did not predict L2 spelling in the present study.

PA was nevertheless related to both real-word and pseudoword outcomes at the bivariate level (r = .32 and r = .25), and it predicted L2 reading comprehension in the model, which is consistent with cross-linguistic transfer of PA from German to English.
Transfer of PA is unlikely to be complete, because PA has both universal and language-specific components.
The ability to attend to and manipulate speech sounds is largely language-independent, but phoneme inventories and sound-to-letter mappings differ between orthographies.
German has a shallow orthography with consistent grapheme-phoneme correspondences, whereas English is deep and contains phonemes absent from German, such as /θ/, /ð/, /æ/, and /ɒ/ (Landerl, 2005).

There were several limitations in our study that warrant consideration.
The pseudoword reading task comprised only 10 monosyllabic items.
Although its internal consistency was acceptable (KR-20 = .71), it is too brief to provide a representative sample of English grapheme-phoneme correspondences and phonemic diversity.
Moreover, our findings regarding the significant predictive effects of L2 grammar on spelling in our regression analyses warrant further investigation.
The ELIAS grammar test we administered covered both morphological elements (e.g., plural -s, 3rd person -s) and syntactic aspects (e.g., Subject-Verb-Object structures, negation, passive forms).
This heterogeneity makes it difficult to draw explicit conclusions about the relative contributions of morphological versus syntactic knowledge to spelling.
Another limitation concerns the language of assessment, as PA was measured only in German.
To more fully understand the role of PA in EFL reading and spelling, future studies should include PA tasks in both the L1 and L2.
WM was also assessed in German, which may have underestimated its potential impact on L2 reading comprehension (Alptekin & Erçetin, 2010).

This limits our interpretation, particularly for oral reading fluency, where limited English print exposure may mean that differences in orthographic learning matter (Share, 1995).

text.text: Another limitation refers to the participant population, which was linguistically heterogeneous: 82 of the 107 learners spoke German at home, and 25 spoke one of 13 other languages.

Due to the lack of a formalized measure of linguistic distance, it was not possible to control for the systematic advantages or challenges that specific L1 backgrounds might pose when acquiring EFL reading and spelling skills.
Lastly, a further limitation concerns the statistical analyses.

The models were based on only five classes, which is a small number of clusters for estimating between-class variance; although the fixed-effect conclusions were supported by using cluster-robust standard errors, the random-effect estimates should be interpreted with caution.

In addition, because the study was not preregistered and multiple predictors were examined across six outcomes, only the effects of NVI and PA on reading comprehension survived correction for multiple testing.
The remaining effects, while consistent with theoretical expectations and prior findings, should be regarded as preliminary and in need of replication.

The pattern differed by outcome.
PA and NVI predicted reading comprehension, with a smaller contribution of L2 vocabulary.
L2 vocabulary and grammar were associated with real-word spelling, whereas NVI was associated with pseudoword spelling, and PSTM with pseudoword reading.
